Q1: Dispatch Call A (Maple St, 7.8). The highest-scored waiting call gets the next available unit even though nothing reaches 9.0, because the threshold triggers escalation, not dispatching. Holding a medic idle while a 7.8 chest-pain call waits would cost critical response time for no valid reason.
Q2: Dispatch Call A (Pine Rd, 8.4). The kitchen fire outscores the dumpster fire 8.4 to 7.9, and the urgency score is the tiebreaker that exists precisely to resolve priority decisions. Below 9.0 there is no mutual aid or command escalation, just normal dispatch of the highest scorer.
Q3: Dispatch Call A (1st St, 8.9). Both calls are just under critical, so the higher score wins: the possible person trapped on the 3rd floor outranks the elevator rescue at 8.8. The near-critical scores do not trigger extra escalation since neither hits 9.0, but dispatch itself never waits for the threshold.
Q4: Dispatch Call A (Hill Rd, 7.1). The diabetic emergency outscores the event standby 7.1 to 5.5, and a scored real medical call always beats a standby request. The 9.0 threshold is an escalation trigger, not a reason to hold the BLS unit idle with a genuine call in the queue.
Q5: Dispatch Call A (River St, 8.1). When scores are nearly tied, the higher score still wins outright, so the breathing difficulty at 8.1 goes before the hip-injury fall at 8.0. A tie does not justify holding; the urgency score is the designed tiebreaker.
Q6: Dispatch Call A (Main St, 6.8). The vehicle fire outscores the brush fire 6.8 to 6.5, and neither reaches 9.0 so the mutual-aid offer is not triggered as escalation. Dispatching the highest scorer to Call A now is correct; mutual aid could be requested separately for Call B.
Q7: Dispatch Call A (Park Ave, 7.5). A multi-vehicle accident with injuries needing command oversight is the only call in the queue, and a single waiting call still gets the unit. Leaving the battalion chief idle when command is needed on scene would be a failure, not prudence.
Q8: Dispatch Call A (Cedar Ln, 8.7). The stroke call wins decisively at 8.7 versus 7.3, and its time-critical treatment window makes immediate dispatch even more important. Below 9.0 there is no escalation trigger, but the medic still goes to the highest-scored call without delay.
Q9: Dispatch Call A (Summit Dr, 5.9). Even though 5.9 is well below the critical threshold, the principle holds: an idle engine with a scored call waiting is a failure. A gas leak in an evacuated home still needs an engine on scene, so dispatch Call A immediately.
